newsitem.title: KENYA: Hutu group says Burundi, Rwandan troops in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Hutu group says Burundi, Rwandan troops in Zaire.

text.p: Burundi's main Hutu rebel group alleged on Friday that some 3,000 Burundian and Rwandan troops were aiding Tutsi rebels in their fight against Zaire's army in eastern Zaire.

Rwanda and Burundi have denied charges this week by Zaire and a Rwandan Hutu refugee lobby group that their troops were fighting alongside the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group which migrated west into what is now Zaire at the end of the 18th century.
Innocent Nimpagaritse, East Africa representative for the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), told a Nairobi news conference:
"The naked truth is that the armies of Burundi and Rwanda have invaded Zaire and are fighting its army," he said.

"They decided to use the Tutsi ethnic group of the Banyamulenge as pretext. We know too well that the Banyamulenge fighting in the 3,000 (strong force) attacking Zaire do not exceed 200 people," he added.
Nimpagaritse said the two armies were backed by heavy artillery including Russian-made multiple rocket launchers.

Western diplomats, while not fully endorsing the CNDD allegations, say the Banyamulenge guerrillas do include veterans of the new Rwandan army. They take seriously accusations by Zaire that many of the rebels were trained and armed by Rwanda in the past 18 months.
During the Rwandan war in 1994 some Banyamulenge left Zaire to join Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated rebel force which is now in power.
On Thursday, an exiled Rwandan Hutu group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda (RDR), said up to 1,800 Rwandan troops were fighting on the side of the Tutsi rebels.
Rwanda swiftly denied the accusations, saying military advances by the Banyamulenge this week were an indication of gross incompetence by the Zairean military.
Diplomats and aid officials fear the fighting in Zaire could spark wider conflict in the Great Lakes region of East Africa.
Eastern Zaire has been a powderkeg since the 1994 civil war and genocide in Rwanda in which up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus died.

More than a million Rwandan Hutus, fearing reprisals for the slaughter in which many of them took part, fled to Zaire. The refugees, including the former government army and extremist militiamen, were housed in U.N. refugee camps close to the borders of Rwanda and Burundi, posing a potential threat to the Tutsi-led governments there.
Some 300,000 Burundian and Rwandan refugees and local Zaireans have fled the recent fighting in eastern Zaire.

Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told a news conference in Brussels on Thursday that Rwandan troups had entered eastern Zaire to help the Tutsi rebels. He also accused Rwanda's army of training guerrilla forces of the Banyamulenge.
